name: CTSpinoPelvic1K
description:
CTSpinoPelvic1K
	

A fused spine + pelvis 3D CT segmentation dataset built by patient-level
crosswalk between three public sources:

TCIA CT COLONOGRAPHY — DICOM CT volumes (prone + supine per patient)
CTSpine1K (COLONOG subset) — VerSe-convention vertebral label masks
CTPelvic1K dataset2 — sacrum + bilateral hip label masks

rai:dataCollection: Patient-level crosswalk of three public datasets: TCIA CT COLONOGRAPHY (de-identified CT volumes, prone and supine acquisitions), CTSpine1K (VerSe-convention vertebral label masks restricted to the COLONOG subset), and CTPelvic1K dataset2 (sacrum and bilateral hip label masks). For each patient, masks are placed onto the TCIA volume with the highest bone coverage (HU > 200), separately per anatomy. LSTV stratification (Normal, Lumbarization, Sacralization, Ambiguous) was assigned by review of lumbosacral morphology. The v20 merged-label scheme assigns a unified L5/L6 label on lumbarization cases to resolve class collision.
rai:dataLimitations: Single-modality CT only; no MRI, radiographic, or clinical correlation is included.
Source cohort is the TCIA CT Colonography screening study, which skews older-adult and US-based; pediatric and non-US populations are absent.
Anatomical coverage is limited to the lumbosacral spine and bony pelvis (sacrum + bilateral hips); cervical spine, full thoracic spine, and lower-extremity structures are not labeled.
Pelvic field-of-view is constrained by the original colonography acquisition protocol.
LSTV strata are imbalanced; sacralization cases in particular are underrepresented relative to Normal and Lumbarization, limiting per-stratum statistical power.
L5/L6 labels in lumbarization cases follow the v20 merged-label convention; downstream users comparing to other vertebral-counting datasets must respect this convention.
Bone-coverage-based volume selection (HU > 200) may behave unexpectedly on low-dose or contrast-enhanced acquisitions.
Inter-source label conventions differ; small residual mismatches at the lumbosacral junction may persist after harmonization.
rai:dataBiases: Indication bias: all source CT volumes were acquired for colon cancer screening, so the cohort skews older (typically 50+) and is enriched for screening-eligible populations.
Geographic bias: TCIA CT Colonography is a predominantly US-based study; non-US populations are not represented.
Demographic bias inherited from the upstream screening cohort, including likely under-representation of younger adults and certain racial/ethnic groups.
Class imbalance across LSTV strata, with sacralization the smallest stratum.
Anatomy bias: the pelvic field-of-view of colonography acquisitions differs from trauma or oncology CT, which may limit transfer to those domains.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: All source data are redistributed from public, de-identified releases (TCIA CT COLONOGRAPHY, CTSpine1K, CTPelvic1K). DICOM headers were stripped of PHI during upstream curation and only NIfTI volumes and label masks are distributed. The spinopelvic field-of-view typically excludes facial anatomy, minimizing re-identification risk from facial reconstruction; where any facial anatomy was incidentally present, defacing was applied. No direct identifiers, dates of service, or institution-level identifiers are retained.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking spinopelvic CT segmentation models, particularly under LSTV anatomical variation.
Training and evaluating LSTV-aware vertebral labeling and counting algorithms.
Research on transitional vertebra detection and Castellvi-style classification.
Auditing existing public segmentation tools (e.g., TotalSegmentator) for failure modes on transitional anatomy.
Educational use for radiology and surgical trainees studying lumbosacral variant anatomy.
NOT intended for direct clinical decision-making, diagnosis, or surgical planning without independent validation and appropriate regulatory clearance.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to mitigate a known and clinically consequential failure mode of existing CT segmentation tools — silent miscounting and mislabeling of vertebrae on patients with lumbosacral transitional vertebrae (LSTV) — that can propagate into surgical-planning and research pipelines. Patients with anatomical variants are systematically underserved by tools trained on 'typical' spines, and improving model robustness on this population is the primary motivation. Foreseeable risks include over-reliance on automated labels in clinical contexts for which the dataset was not designed, and amplification of upstream demographic biases (older-adult, US-based screening cohort) if models trained on it are deployed without site-specific validation.
